The optimal tip-speed ratio for cross-flow turbines is not explicitly stated.
Power generation from the upstream sweep continues to increase beyond the optimal tip-speed ratio.
The downstream sweep consumes power beyond the optimal tip-speed ratio due to unfavorable lift and drag directions.
Induction modifies the nominal kinematics, leading to differences in the angle of attack and relative velocity between the upstream and downstream sweeps.
Dynamic stall is a non-linear phenomenon that can lead to performance degradation in the downstream sweep.
The upstream sweep contributes the most to power production, but the downstream sweep determines the optimal tip-speed ratio.
The preset pitch angle affects the maximum angle of attack magnitude in the upstream and downstream sweeps.
The Reynolds number affects the performance of cross-flow turbines, with higher Reynolds numbers leading to improved performance.
The experimental setup consists of a one-bladed turbine and a particle image velocimetry (PIV) system.
The tip-speed ratios used in the experiments are λ = 1.4, 2.4, and 3.4.
The blockage ratio affects the performance of cross-flow turbines, with higher blockage ratios leading to reduced performance.
The chord-to-radius ratio affects the performance of cross-flow turbines, with higher ratios leading to improved performance.
The nominal angle of attack and relative velocity do not accurately represent the true angle of attack and relative velocity due to induction.
The angle of attack range experienced by the blade affects the severity of dynamic stall.
The near-blade flow structures differ substantially between the upstream and downstream sweeps.
The topology of the near-blade flow structures is affected by the angle of attack range and the Reynolds number.
The induction-modified inflow affects the true relative velocity magnitude and the true angle of attack.
The true relative velocity magnitude and the true angle of attack vary with blade azimuthal position.
